title: False friends and first expressions
topic: frequent false friends and everyday expressions
why: Before the big review of the basics, this lesson clears up the false friends that trip up every English speaker (actuellement, librairie, assister, sensible…) and gives you the little expressions French people use all day long. No new grammar: just words that make you sound natural and keep you out of trouble.

False friends: words that lie

French and English share thousands of words: la table, important, possible, la question… Most of the time, that's a gift. But a handful of very common words look English and mean something else. The French call them les faux amis, \"false friends\", and they cause the funniest misunderstandings.

French wordWhat it really meansFor the English word, say…
actuellementcurrently, at the momentactually → en fait
une librairiea bookshoplibrary → une bibliothèque
assister àto attendto assist → aider
resterto stayto rest → se reposer
une locationa rentala location → un endroit
la monnaiechange (coins)money → l'argent
une vestea jacketa vest → un gilet
un cara coach, an intercity busa car → une voiture

The worst one is probably actuellement. When an English speaker says \"actually\", a French person hears \"at the moment\". To say \"actually\", use en fait.

Actuellement, je travaille à Lyon.At the moment, I work in Lyon.
En fait, je n'aime pas le café.Actually, I don't like coffee.
Je veux acheter un livre : il y a une librairie près d'ici ?I want to buy a book: is there a bookshop near here?
Demain, j'assiste à une réunion à neuf heures.Tomorrow, I'm attending a meeting at nine.
Vous avez de la monnaie sur vingt euros ?Do you have change for twenty euros?

Rester never means \"to rest\": Je reste à la maison ce soir = I'm staying home tonight. To rest is se reposer, which you know from your daily routine: Le dimanche, je me repose.

", "

More traps: sensible, éventuellement, journée…

A second group of false friends is more subtle: the meaning isn't completely different, but it has shifted.

  • sensible = sensitive (easily hurt, or delicate). \"Sensible\" in the English sense is raisonnable.
  • éventuellement = possibly, if need be. It never means \"eventually\", which is closer to finalement (a word you'll meet again soon).
  • formidable = great, wonderful. It's purely positive, never scary or impressive in a threatening way.
  • dur = hard, in both senses: not soft, and difficult. Travailler dur = to work hard; C'est dur ! = It's tough!
Ma fille est très sensible : elle n'aime pas les films tristes.My daughter is very sensitive: she doesn't like sad movies.
Tu es raisonnable : tu ne sors pas ce soir.You're sensible: you're not going out tonight.
On peut éventuellement dîner plus tard.We can possibly have dinner later.
Le spectacle est formidable !The show is wonderful!

Un jour or une journée?

English has one word, \"day\". French has two. Le jour is the day as a unit or a date; la journée is the day as a stretch of time, with everything you do in it. The same pattern exists for le soir / la soirée (evening) and le matin / la matinée (morning).

le jour: a unit, a datela journée: the whole day, its content
trois jours, quel jour, le jour de mon anniversaireBonne journée !, toute la journée, une journée difficile

When a long English word ends in -tion, -ible or -able, it usually means the same in French: une réservation, possible, confortable. The false friends are a short list: learn them as exceptions, and trust the other look-alikes.

", "

Everyday expressions

These little phrases are everywhere in France. They make your French sound natural immediately, and they cost no grammar at all.

ExpressionMeaningWhen to use it
d'accordOK, all rightto agree, in any situation
ça marchesounds good, OKcasual; waiters say it too
pas de soucino problemcasual and very frequent
ça ne fait riennever mind, it doesn't matterwhen something small goes wrong
ce n'est pas graveit's no big deal, don't worryto answer an apology
bon appétitenjoy your mealbefore eating, to everyone at the table
à tout à l'heuresee you later (today)when you'll meet again the same day
à plus tard, à plussee you latercasual; in texts, A+
oh là làoh dear, wowsurprise, annoyance, admiration
bofmehnot impressed, not really
ça dépendit dependswhen you can't answer yes or no
—Pardon, je n'ai pas de monnaie. —Ce n'est pas grave.—Sorry, I don't have any change. —Don't worry about it.
—On dîne à huit heures ? —Ça marche !—Shall we have dinner at eight? —Sounds good!
—Tu aimes ce film ? —Bof…—Do you like this movie? —Meh…

In speech, ce n'est pas grave often becomes c'est pas grave, without ne. You'll hear it all the time, but write the full form. In à plus, the final s is pronounced. And oh là là has nothing to do with romance: it's what a French person says when the train is cancelled.

La bise

Friends and family greet each other with la bise, a light kiss on each cheek (faire la bise). Two kisses in Paris, sometimes three or four in other regions. With strangers and in professional settings, people shake hands.

In Quebec, c'est correct means \"it's fine, it's OK\". In France, correct means \"correct, acceptable\": say ça va or pas de souci instead.
